key_terms.meaning: A switch that repeatedly connects and disconnects a DC source to a load so the average load voltage is set by the on-time fraction.
D = T<sub>on</sub>/T, the fraction of one switching period T that the switch is on; 0 ≤ D ≤ 1.
A chopper control method that turns the switch off at a set peak current and on again when current falls to a lower limit.
A chopper control method that changes switching frequency while keeping on-time or off-time fixed, so D and average voltage change.
A regulator that uses a pass transistor in its linear region to drop excess input voltage as heat.
A supply that chops the input and uses inductors, capacitors and a controller to regulate output at high efficiency.
A step-down converter with a switch-diode pair before an L-C filter; in CCM, V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub>.
CCM: the inductor current stays above zero throughout the switching period.
A step-up converter that stores inductor energy with the switch on and delivers it in series with the source; in CCM, V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D).
A converter that stores and then delivers inductor energy with reversed output polarity; in CCM, V<sub>o</sub> = −V<sub>s</sub>·D/(1 − D).
A converter with a capacitor as the energy-transfer element, giving the same gain magnitude as buck-boost with smoother port currents.
An isolated converter that stores energy in the transformer during on-time and delivers it to the output during off-time.
An isolated converter that transfers energy to the output during switch on-time and needs a core-reset method each cycle.
n = N1/N2, the primary-to-secondary turns ratio in the flyback gain V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>·D/((1 − D)·n).
A converter that uses an L-C resonant tank to shape switch voltage or current and reduce switching loss.
ZVS: turning a switch on after its voltage has fallen to zero, removing the turn-on overlap loss and the C<sub>oss</sub> discharge loss.
ZCS: changing switch state when its current is near zero, removing voltage-current overlap loss.
Peak-to-peak inductor current; for a buck in CCM, ΔI<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>o</sub>(1 − D)/(L·f<sub>s</sub>).
Equivalent series resistance that turns capacitor ripple current into ripple voltage ΔV ≈ ΔI<sub>C</sub> × ESR and causes internal heating.
A short non-magnetic gap in a magnetic core that stores energy and sets inductance and saturation margin.

takeaways: A chopper sets average DC output by duty cycle, not by dissipating excess voltage as heat.
A linear regulator is simple and quiet but wastes (1 − efficiency) of input power as heat; an SMPS chops and filters for 70–95 % efficiency with ripple and EMI penalties.
The buck converter gives V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub> in CCM, and its inductor ripple sets the inductance and output-capacitor requirement.
The boost converter gives V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D) in CCM, so the output is always higher than the input and D must stay away from 1.
The buck-boost converter inverts the output and gives V<sub>o</sub> = −V<sub>s</sub>·D/(1 − D); the Cuk converter gives the same gain magnitude with smoother port currents.
A flyback stores energy in the transformer during on-time and delivers it during off-time; a forward converter delivers during on-time and must reset the core.
High switching frequency shrinks magnetics but raises switching loss; resonant soft switching reduces loss by forcing zero voltage or zero current before a transition.
Inductor and transformer design keeps peak flux density, current density and temperature inside limits; capacitor ESR often sets the real output ripple.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for the circuit, the CCM gain derivation, the switch-diode-inductor waveforms and a design or loss check with clear units.

bank.q: Define duty cycle and explain how a chopper controls the average DC voltage across a resistive load. Give the average-voltage formula and name two control methods.
outline: D = T<sub>on</sub>/T and T = 1/f<sub>s</sub>
Switch on connects source to load; switch off disconnects it
Average load voltage V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub>; RMS V<sub>s</sub>√D and power D·V<sub>s</sub>²/R for a resistive load
Current-limit control and variable-frequency control named correctly
answer: Circuit: a DC source V<sub>s</sub>, a fast switch S (MOSFET or IGBT with its gate driver) and the load R in series. With an inductive load a freewheeling diode D<sub>f</sub> sits across the load to carry its current when S opens.

Switching: S is closed for T<sub>on</sub> and open for T<sub>off</sub>, and the pattern repeats every period T = T<sub>on</sub> + T<sub>off</sub> = 1/f<sub>s</sub>. With S closed the load is tied to the source, v<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>; with S open, v<sub>o</sub> = 0 (about −0.7 V while D<sub>f</sub> conducts). The load voltage is a pulse train of height V<sub>s</sub>.
Duty cycle: D = T<sub>on</sub>/T = T<sub>on</sub>·f<sub>s</sub>, the fraction of each period the switch is on, so 0 ≤ D ≤ 1.

answer.text: Average load voltage, by averaging the pulse train over one period:
answer.pre:
V<sub>o</sub> = (1/T) ∫₀ᵀ v<sub>o</sub> dt = (1/T)(V<sub>s</sub>·T<sub>on</sub> + 0·T<sub>off</sub>)
    = V<sub>s</sub>·T<sub>on</sub>/T = D·V<sub>s</sub>

answer: So the chopper controls the average voltage by the on-time fraction alone; it does not drop the excess across a resistor. At D = 0 the load gets nothing, at D = 1 the full V<sub>s</sub>. The RMS value of the same pulse train is V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√D, and for a purely resistive load the power is P<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>rms</sub>²/R = D·V<sub>s</sub>²/R.

answer: Assumptions: ideal switch and diode, continuous conduction (i<sub>L</sub> never reaches zero), steady state, and C large enough that V<sub>o</sub> is constant over a cycle. D = T<sub>on</sub>/T and T = 1/f<sub>s</sub>.

Switch ON (0 < t < DT): D<sub>f</sub> is reverse biased because its cathode is at V<sub>s</sub>. The inductor connects the source to the output, so v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>, a positive constant: i<sub>L</sub> rises in a straight line with slope (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)/L. Energy goes into L and the load.

Switch OFF (DT < t < T): i<sub>L</sub> cannot stop, so D<sub>f</sub> turns on and the inductor now runs from the return rail to the output: v<sub>L</sub> = −V<sub>o</sub>. i<sub>L</sub> falls with slope −V<sub>o</sub>/L while L supplies the load.

answer.text: Volt-second balance: in steady state i<sub>L</sub> ends each period where it started, so the average of v<sub>L</sub> over a period is zero.
answer.pre:
(V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)·DT + (−V<sub>o</sub>)·(1 − D)T = 0
D·V<sub>s</sub> − D·V<sub>o</sub> − V<sub>o</sub> + D·V<sub>o</sub> = 0
V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub>

answer: Since D ≤ 1, V<sub>o</sub> ≤ V<sub>s</sub>: the buck only steps down, and the gain is set by D, not by burning voltage.

answer.text: Ripple current, from the on-state ramp:
answer.pre:
ΔI<sub>L</sub> = (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)·DT/L
with V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>(1 − D) and D·V<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>o</sub>:
ΔI<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>o</sub>(1 − D)/(f<sub>s</sub>·L)

svg.aria: Boost converter: source, inductor L, switch S to the return rail, diode D1 to capacitor C and load R.

answer: Assumptions: ideal parts, continuous conduction, steady state, V<sub>o</sub> constant over a cycle; D = T<sub>on</sub>/T.

Switch ON (for DT): the switch shorts the inductor’s far end to the rail, so the full source voltage is across L: v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>. i<sub>L</sub> rises with slope V<sub>s</sub>/L and energy builds up in L. D1 is reverse biased (its cathode is at V<sub>o</sub>) and C alone feeds the load.

Switch OFF (for (1 − D)T): i<sub>L</sub> cannot stop, so the node voltage rises until D1 conducts. Now the source and the inductor are in series driving the output: v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>, which is negative, so i<sub>L</sub> falls while L hands its stored energy to C and R.

answer.text: Volt-second balance on L:
answer.pre:
V<sub>s</sub>·DT + (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)(1 − D)T = 0
V<sub>s</sub> − (1 − D)V<sub>o</sub> = 0
V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D)

answer: Why V<sub>o</sub> > V<sub>s</sub>: for 0 < D < 1 the factor 1/(1 − D) is greater than 1. Physically, during the off-time the inductor’s voltage adds to the source voltage, because L reverses its voltage to keep its current flowing. answer: Why the core must reset: while the switch is on, V<sub>s</sub> across the primary drives the magnetizing flux up by a volt-second product V<sub>s</sub>·D·T. The forward’s transformer is not meant to store energy, so before the next cycle that flux must come back to its starting value; otherwise it climbs a little every cycle until the core saturates and the switch current spikes.

How the reset winding works: N<sub>r</sub> is wound on the same core with its diode connected back to the input. At turn-off the magnetizing current transfers to N<sub>r</sub>, the diode conducts and puts −V<sub>s</sub>·(N<sub>p</sub>/N<sub>r</sub>) across the primary; the magnetizing energy is returned to the source, not burnt.

svg.aria: Three circuits stacked: the buck, the boost and the inverting buck-boost converter, each with its gain.

answer.text: Comparison table:

answer: Derivations in one line each, from volt-second balance on L: buck (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)D = V<sub>o</sub>(1 − D); boost V<sub>s</sub>·D = (V<sub>o</sub> − V<sub>s</sub>)(1 − D); buck-boost V<sub>s</sub>·D = |V<sub>o</sub>|(1 − D).
Battery to a 5 V rail: the answer depends on the battery voltage range, so work it out for two common cases.

answer.text: A 12 V lead-acid battery (about 10.5 V flat to 14.4 V charging): always above 5 V, so a buck.
answer.pre:
D = 5/14.4 = 0.347 at full charge
D = 5/10.5 = 0.476 when flat

answer: The buck gives the lowest stresses (the switch blocks only the battery voltage) and a smooth output current into the 5 V load. A buck-boost would also work but its switch would block 14.4 + 5 = 19.4 V and its output would be −5 V.

answer.text: One lithium-ion cell (3.0 V to 4.2 V): always below 5 V, so a boost.
answer.pre:
D = 1 − 3.0/5 = 0.40 when nearly empty
D = 1 − 4.2/5 = 0.16 when full

answer.text: Stresses at a 12 V battery and a 5 V, 2 A load, buck against inverting buck-boost:

answer: The buck-boost carries 42 % more inductor current and blocks 42 % more voltage for the same job, so its losses and parts are larger.

If the battery range crosses 5 V (for example four NiMH cells, about 4.0 V to 5.6 V), neither the buck nor the boost alone works; a non-inverting buck-boost (SEPIC or a four-switch buck-boost) is used, because the plain buck-boost would give a negative rail.

Conclusion for the usual case of a battery above 5 V: the buck, with D between 0.35 and 0.48, the smallest device stresses and the best efficiency. Check: 0.347 × 14.4 = 5.0 V and 0.476 × 10.5 = 5.0 V; 3.0/(1 − 0.4) = 5.0 V.

bank.q: A 100 W converter must switch at 500 kHz to shrink magnetics. Explain the switching-loss problem and how ZVS or ZCS reduces it. Include the roles of snubbers and a resonant tank.
outline: High f<sub>s</sub> increases loss per switching transition × f<sub>s</sub>
Voltage-current overlap causes turn-on and turn-off loss
ZVS makes switch voltage zero before turn-on; ZCS makes current zero before turn-off
Resonant tank shapes voltage or current; snubber limits spikes and shapes trajectory
Trade-off: extra resonant components and higher conduction or circulating loss
answer: Take a 100 W off-line stage with a 400 V bus, so the switch carries about I = 0.5 A, with voltage and current transitions of 20 ns each (t<sub>r</sub> + t<sub>f</sub> = 40 ns) and an output capacitance C<sub>oss</sub> = 100 pF. These are typical assumed values, used to show the trend.

answer.text: Hard-switching loss at 100 kHz and at 500 kHz:

answer: The problem: every transition costs a fixed energy, so the switching loss rises in proportion to f<sub>s</sub>. Raising the frequency five times to shrink the magnetics multiplies this loss by five, and the heat sink grows back. The overlap loss comes from the device holding voltage and carrying current at the same time; the C<sub>oss</sub> loss comes from the capacitance being dumped into the channel at each turn-on.

ZVS: a resonant tank (or the magnetizing current of a transformer) discharges C<sub>oss</sub> before the gate pulse, the body diode clamps the switch voltage at zero, and the channel turns on with v = 0. Both the turn-on overlap and the ½·C<sub>oss</sub>·V²·f<sub>s</sub> term disappear. At 500 kHz that removes 1.0 W of turn-on overlap and 4.0 W of C<sub>oss</sub> loss, leaving 1.0 W, and a small capacitor across the switch slows the voltage rise at turn-off so most of the remaining 1.0 W goes too.

ZCS: the tank brings the switch current to zero before the gate is removed, so the device turns off with i = 0 and the turn-off overlap disappears. It suits IGBTs and thyristors, whose tail current makes turn-off the costly transition, but the C<sub>oss</sub> loss at turn-on stays.

answer.text: The resonant tank: L<sub>r</sub> and C<sub>r</sub> set the natural frequency, chosen near the switching frequency.
answer.pre:
f<sub>0</sub> = 1/(2π√(L<sub>r</sub>·C<sub>r</sub>))
L<sub>r</sub> = 10 µH, C<sub>r</sub> = 10 nF: f<sub>0</sub> = 1/(2π × √(10⁻⁵ × 10⁻⁸)) = 503 kHz

answer: Snubbers: an RC or RCD snubber across a hard-switched device limits dv/dt and the voltage spike from leakage inductance and shapes the switching trajectory, but its capacitor energy ½CV² is burnt in the resistor every cycle, so it moves loss out of the device rather than removing it. A lossless or resonant snubber returns that energy instead, which is the step towards soft switching.

Trade-offs: the tank adds parts and circulating current, so the RMS current and conduction loss rise; ZVS is lost at light load when the tank current is too small to discharge C<sub>oss</sub>; and the output is usually controlled by frequency, not duty ratio, which narrows the regulation range.
Check: ½ × 400 × 0.5 × 40 ns × 500 kHz = 2.0 W and ½ × 100 pF × 400² × 500 kHz = 4.0 W, five times the 100 kHz values of 0.4 W and 0.8 W.

bank.q: For a 24 V to 12 V, 5 A buck at 200 kHz, choose L for 30 % ripple, choose C for 50 mV ripple ignoring ESR, and check the ESR and inductor saturation limits. Explain each limit.
outline: L = V<sub>o</sub>(1 − D)/(ΔI<sub>L</sub>·f<sub>s</sub>) = 20 μH
C = ΔI<sub>L</sub>/(8·f<sub>s</sub>·ΔV<sub>o</sub>) = 18.75 μF
ESR must be below 50 mV/1.5 A = 33.3 mΩ
Inductor saturation current must exceed peak 5.75 A
answer: Data: V<sub>s</sub> = 24 V, V<sub>o</sub> = 12 V, I<sub>o</sub> = 5 A, f<sub>s</sub> = 200 kHz; ripple current 30 % of I<sub>o</sub>; output ripple 50 mV.

answer.text: Duty ratio and inductor:

answer: Limit 1, ripple and CCM: the inductor current swings from 5 − 0.75 = 4.25 A to 5 + 0.75 = 5.75 A. The converter stays in CCM down to I<sub>o</sub> = ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2 = 0.75 A; below that load it enters DCM and the gain changes.

answer.text: Capacitor, ignoring ESR:
answer.pre:
C = ΔI<sub>L</sub>/(8 f<sub>s</sub> ΔV<sub>o</sub>) = 1.5/(8 × 200 000 × 0.05) = 18.75 µF → 22 µF
capacitive ripple with 22 µF: 1.5/(8 × 200 000 × 22 µF) = 42.6 mV

answer.text: Limit 2, ESR: the ripple current ΔI<sub>L</sub> also flows through the capacitor’s ESR, adding ΔI<sub>L</sub> × ESR.
answer.pre:
ESR alone may not exceed 50 mV/1.5 A = 33.3 mΩ
with 22 µF: ESR ≤ (50 − 42.6)/1.5 = 4.9 mΩ (ceramic only)
with 47 µF: capacitive part 19.9 mV, ESR ≤ (50 − 19.9)/1.5 = 20 mΩ

answer: So pick 47 µF of low-ESR capacitors (for example ceramics in parallel) rather than the bare 18.75 µF. The capacitor’s RMS ripple current is ΔI<sub>L</sub>/√12 = 0.43 A, which must be within its rating.

Limit 3, inductor saturation: the core must carry the peak, not the average. I<sub>pk</sub> = 5.75 A, so choose an inductor whose saturation current is above about 7 A (20 % margin), with copper for I<sub>rms</sub> = √(5² + 1.5²/12) = 5.02 A.

answer.text: Inductor build, if wound on a gapped ferrite core with A<sub>e</sub> = 0.5 cm² and B<sub>max</sub> = 0.3 T:
answer.pre:
N = L·I<sub>pk</sub>/(B<sub>max</sub>·A<sub>e</sub>) = 20 µH × 5.75/(0.3 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁴) = 7.7 → 8 turns
B = 20 µH × 5.75/(8 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.29 T
ℓ<sub>g</sub> = µ₀N²A<sub>e</sub>/L = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 64 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁴/20 µH = 0.20 mm
A<sub>cu</sub> = 5.02/4 A/mm² = 1.25 mm²

answer.text: Design summary:

answer: Why each limit matters: too little L gives a large ripple and early DCM; too little C or too much ESR gives an output ripple above specification; a saturating core loses its inductance at the peak, so the current spikes and can destroy the switch.

glossary.def: A power electronic switch or circuit that repeatedly connects and disconnects a DC source to a load to control average voltage or current.
The ratio D = T<sub>on</sub>/T of switch on-time to switching period, ranging from 0 to 1.
f<sub>s</sub> = 1/T, the number of on-off cycles per second, in hertz.
A chopper control method that switches off at a set maximum current and switches on again when current falls to a lower limit.
A chopper control method that changes f<sub>s</sub> while keeping on-time or off-time fixed, so D and average voltage change.
A regulator that uses a pass transistor in its linear region to drop excess input voltage as heat.
The series transistor in a linear regulator that carries load current and dissipates the unused voltage.
The minimum input-to-output voltage difference a linear regulator needs to keep regulating.
A power supply that chops the input and uses inductors, capacitors and a controller to regulate output with high efficiency.
The small periodic variation on a DC output caused by switching and finite energy storage.
Electromagnetic interference, unwanted high-frequency noise that switching converters can conduct or radiate.
CCM: inductor current never falls to zero during a switching period.
DCM: inductor current stays at zero for part of each switching period.
A step-down DC-DC converter whose ideal CCM gain is V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub>.
A step-up DC-DC converter whose ideal CCM gain is V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D).
An inverting converter whose ideal CCM gain is V<sub>o</sub> = −V<sub>s</sub>·D/(1 − D).
A converter with capacitor energy transfer, gain magnitude D/(1 − D), inverted output and low port current ripple.
An isolated converter that stores energy in transformer magnetizing inductance during on-time and delivers it during off-time.
An isolated converter that transfers energy through the transformer during on-time and must reset the core each cycle.
An extra transformer winding that returns magnetizing energy to the source and resets core flux in a forward converter.
ZVS: switching a device when its voltage is near zero.
ZCS: switching a device when its current is near zero.
A non-magnetic gap in a core that increases energy storage and prevents saturation.
Equivalent series resistance; it makes ripple current produce ripple voltage and internal heating.
A small R-C or R-D network across a switch or diode that limits voltage or current spikes and shapes switching trajectories.
